_note: Name-facts for South Korea (FT-41, docs/PLAN_V0.9.md). See italy.json
Korean province names are almost all portmanteaus: each takes the first
syllable of its two most important towns and joins them. Chungcheong is
Chungju + Cheongju, Gyeongsang is Gyeongju + Sangju, Jeolla is Jeonju +
Naju, Gangwon is Gangneung + Wonju. Say that once and four of the
eight stop being noise. The other names are mostly Sino-Korean
descriptions - do = province, buk = north, nam = south, san = mountain,
ju = a district or town, cheon/gang = river.
gangwon: Gangneung plus Wonju — the two big towns of the east, their first syllables joined, as with most Korean provinces.
The most mountainous province and the least populated; the DMZ runs along its northern edge, cutting the historic province in half.
Pyeongchang here held the 2018 Winter Olympics.
seoul: Unusual among Korean place names in being pure native Korean rather than Sino-Korean: seoul simply means "capital", so the city is called Capital.
It has been the capital since 1394, and about half of all South Koreans live in it or its surrounding region.
Its subway is one of the busiest and longest in the world, and the city was almost entirely rebuilt after the Korean War flattened it.
gyeonggi: "The area around the capital" — gyeong is capital, gi the surrounding district; the name only makes sense with Seoul in the middle of it.
The most populous province, and it wraps completely around Seoul and Incheon.
Suwon's Hwaseong fortress in it was built in the 1790s using a crane its designer invented, and is a UNESCO site.
incheon: "Kind river" in Sino-Korean, though the older name was Michuhol; the modern name dates from 1413.
MacArthur's 1950 landing here turned the Korean War, and the tides that made it risky are among the largest in Asia.
Its airport is regularly rated the best in the world and is built on land reclaimed between two islands.
north-chungcheong: Chungju plus Cheongju, north half — the portmanteau rule again.
The only landlocked province in the country.
Its Beopjusa temple holds a 33 m gilt-bronze Buddha, and the Cheongju Early Printing Museum marks the Jikji of 1377, printed with movable metal type 78 years before Gutenberg.
sejong: Named for King Sejong, who invented the Korean alphabet in 1443 — the only province-level unit named after a person.
Created in 2012 as a planned administrative capital, to move ministries out of Seoul.
Hangul, Sejong's alphabet, was designed so the letter shapes show how the mouth makes the sound, and is often called the most scientific writing system in use.
north-gyeongsang: Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom for a thousand years and is called a museum without walls.
Andong in it keeps Korea's Confucian traditions most strongly, and its mask dance and village are UNESCO-listed.
south-chungcheong: Baekje, the kingdom that carried Buddhism and writing to Japan, had its capitals here at Gongju and Buyeo.
Its west coast mudflats are a major stop for migratory shorebirds on the East Asian flyway.
daejeon: "Big field" — daejeon is the Sino-Korean reading of an older native name, Hanbat, meaning exactly the same thing.
It was a village until the railway arrived in 1905 and is now the country's science city, with dozens of government research institutes.
Its Daedeok cluster developed much of Korea's semiconductor and telecoms research.
daegu: "Big hill", from the Sino-Korean characters for large and hill.
It sits in a basin and is the hottest city in Korea, regularly the summer record-holder.
Korea's textile industry grew here, and its medicinal herb market has traded since 1658.
north-jeolla: Jeonju is the ancestral seat of the Joseon royal house and the home of bibimbap; its hanok village has some 700 traditional houses.
The province grows the rice of the Honam plain, historically the country's granary.
ulsan: "Mountain of Ul", after an older local name.
It has the highest income per head in Korea: Hyundai's shipyard here is the largest in the world, and its car plant among the largest.
The Bangudae petroglyphs nearby show whale hunting carved about 7,000 years ago — some of the earliest evidence of whaling anywhere.
south-gyeongsang: Admiral Yi Sun-sin beat the Japanese fleet repeatedly in these waters in the 1590s, at odds of ten to one and more.
Its Haeinsa temple holds the Tripitaka Koreana, 81,000 woodblocks carved in the 1200s and still uncracked in a hall designed to keep them dry.
gwangju: "Bright district" — gwang is light, ju a district.
The 1980 uprising here against military rule was crushed with hundreds killed, and is now the founding story of South Korean democracy.
The city holds Asia's oldest contemporary art biennale, started in 1995 in memory of those events.
busan: "Cauldron mountain", for a peak behind the city said to look like an upturned pot.
The second city and the country's great port, and the only major city the North never took — it held the Pusan Perimeter in 1950.
Its Jagalchi fish market is Korea's largest, and its film festival is the most important in Asia.
south-jeolla: It has over 2,000 islands, more than half of all the islands in South Korea.
Boseong's tea terraces and the Suncheon Bay wetlands are both here, and the province produces most of the country's seaweed.
jeju: "The district across" — je is to cross over, ju a district: the island over the water.
A shield volcano: Hallasan at 1,947 m is South Korea's highest point, and the island's lava tubes are a UNESCO site.
Its haenyeo, women who free-dive for shellfish into their seventies without breathing apparatus, are on the UNESCO intangible heritage list.
chuncheon: The capital of Gangwon, on a lake formed by dams on the Bukhan river.
Dakgalbi, stir-fried spicy chicken, was invented here in the 1960s as cheap food for soldiers and students.
gangneung: "River hill" — one half of the portmanteau that makes the province name Gangwon.
The coastal venues for the 2018 Winter Olympics were here.
Its Danoje festival, a shamanic rite going back centuries, is a UNESCO intangible heritage item.
goyang: "High sun" or "high brightness", from the merging of two older districts.
A satellite city of Seoul, and the site of KINTEX, Korea’s largest exhibition centre.
Its Haengju fortress saw a 1593 battle in which civilians, including women carrying stones in their aprons, helped repel a Japanese force.
bucheon: Squeezed between Seoul and Incheon, it is one of the most densely populated cities in the country.
It is a UNESCO City of Literature and hosts a well-known fantastic film festival.
seongnam: "South of the fortress" — seong fortress, nam south.
Bundang in it was one of Korea’s first planned new towns, built in the early 1990s.
Pangyo beside it is the country’s main software cluster, often called the Korean Silicon Valley.
wonju: "Field district" — the other half of the Gangwon portmanteau.
Its Chiaksan national park has some of the steepest hiking in the country.
The Goryeo-era woodblocks of the Tripitaka were first carved in this region before being moved south.
ansan: It has one of the largest foreign-born populations in Korea, with a multicultural district serving dozens of nationalities.
The Sewol ferry disaster of 2014 killed 250 students from a single high school here.
suwon: Its Hwaseong fortress was built in the 1790s by a king for his father’s tomb, using a crane its designer invented, and is a UNESCO site.
Samsung Electronics has its main research campus in the city.
cheongju: "Clear district" — one half of the Chungcheong portmanteau.
The Jikji, printed here in 1377 with movable metal type, is 78 years older than the Gutenberg Bible and is a UNESCO Memory of the World item.
The temple that printed it is gone; only its site and the book, now in Paris, survive.
andong: It is the most Confucian city in Korea, and its Hahoe village and mask dance are both UNESCO-listed.
Andong soju, distilled here since the Goryeo period, is far stronger than the modern industrial kind.
pohang: "Encircling bay" — po a bay or inlet.
POSCO here is one of the largest steelmakers in the world, built from nothing in 1968 with Japanese reparations money.
Homigot on its cape has a giant bronze hand rising from the sea, where Koreans watch the year’s first sunrise.
gunsan: "Group mountain" — gun a group, san mountain, for the islands offshore.
It was a rice-export port under Japanese rule, and more Japanese colonial buildings survive here than anywhere in Korea.
Its Saemangeum seawall is the longest in the world at 33 km.
iksan: Mireuksa here was the largest Buddhist temple in Baekje, and its stone pagoda is the oldest and biggest in Korea.
A gilt-bronze reliquary found inside it in 2009 rewrote what was known about the temple’s founding.
gyeongju: "Capital district" — gyeong capital, the same character as in Gyeonggi.
It was the capital of the Silla kingdom for a thousand years and is called a museum without walls.
Seokguram grotto and Bulguksa temple above it are UNESCO sites, and royal tomb mounds sit among the streets.
jeonju: "Perfect district" — one half of the Jeolla portmanteau.
It is the ancestral seat of the Joseon royal house and a UNESCO City of Gastronomy.
Bibimbap is its dish, and its hanok village has about 700 traditional tiled houses.
changwon: "Prosperous field" — chang to flourish, won a field.
Korea’s first planned industrial city, laid out in the 1970s for heavy machinery.
It introduced the country’s first public bicycle-sharing scheme and has unusually wide, green streets.
mokpo: "Wood port" — mok wood, po a port.
The gateway to the thousands of islands of the south-west, with ferries to most of them.
The Sewol ferry was raised and brought here in 2017; its hull is kept as a memorial.
yeosu: Admiral Yi Sun-sin based his fleet here, and replicas of his ironclad turtle ships are moored in the harbour.
It hosted the 2012 World Expo on the theme of the ocean.
